Sampled HR@10 with one positive and 99 negatives measures retrieval within 100 candidates; it does not estimate full-catalog HR@10 directly. Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model ordering even in expectation. Li et al. find useful correspondence through a mapping to a different full-catalog cutoff, which does not establish equivalence at K=10. Implication: optimize the pinned sampled benchmark, but avoid interpreting improvements as full-catalog top-10 gains. [Krichene–Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/), [Li et al.](https://www.kdd.org/kdd2020/accepted-papers/view/on-sampling-top-k-recommendation-evaluation.html).

For this panel, adapt paired bootstrap resampling: retain each user’s hit indicators for both models, resample the same user indices within each category, and recompute the four-category macro-average difference. Report its confidence interval and category differences. This preserves pairing and equal category weights. Calculated resolution: one changed hit moves category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points. User bootstrap estimates uncertainty conditional on fitted models and fixed candidate sets; it does not capture candidate-resampling or training-seed variation. [Paired-bootstrap methodology](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/).

Repeatedly selecting architectures, hyperparameters and checkpoints on these same users and candidates can overfit validation noise; the winning score becomes optimistic. Cawley and Talbot show finite-sample model-selection variance can cause substantial selection bias. Practical implication within the budget: prioritize a small hypothesis-driven search, inspect paired gains across categories, and treat small improvements cautiously. Ordinary bootstrap intervals after adaptive selection do not remove selection bias; preserve the independent held-out evaluation for the final assessment. [Cawley–Talbot](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume11/cawley10a/cawley10a.pdf).
